entry.title: Umbrellas in a cage
entry.content:
A molecule of ammonia, started in one shape, tunnels inside out and back about twenty-four billion times a second, through an energy barrier it does not have enough energy to climb. This post is about two of its cousins, and about what happens to that flip when you lock the molecule inside a cage of sixty carbon atoms.

The paper this post is about asks a narrow question: if you take a small, pyramid-shaped molecule that likes to flip inside out, and shut it inside a C₆₀ fullerene, does the flip get easier or harder, and why? We looked at two molecules, the hydronium ion (OH₃⁺, the thing that makes acids acidic) and phosphine (PH₃), and the answer turned out to be different for each . The work was done at Krea University with Dr Brijesh Kumar Mishra and Dr Sivakumar Srinivasan, together with Shreya Chidambaram and Netra Krishna.

I came to this project without having done any quantum chemistry. I had to teach myself how to use ORCA, what a basis set was, why there were dozens of “functionals” with names like B3LYP and M06-2X, and how to keep a cluster busy without breaking it. So this post is written for someone in roughly the position I was in: you have done some physics and chemistry, you have heard the words “quantum tunnelling” and “DFT”, and you would like to know what they actually mean. The first third builds up the idea of inversion and tunnelling, the middle third is a tour of how molecules are calculated, and the last third puts the two together to read the paper’s results. The practical side, how I learned ORCA and ran these jobs on a cluster, will get a post of its own.

An umbrella in the wind

Ammonia, NH₃, is shaped like a short, squat pyramid: a nitrogen atom on top, three hydrogens forming the base. The nitrogen also carries a pair of electrons that are not shared with anything, a “lone pair”, which sits on the side away from the hydrogens and pushes them down, a bit like the canopy of an umbrella with the handle being the lone pair.

Now imagine the umbrella in a strong wind. The canopy goes flat, and then pops through to the other side. A pyramidal molecule can do the same thing: the central atom passes through the plane of the three hydrogens and comes out on the other side, and you end up with the same pyramid, pointing the other way. This is called umbrella inversion, and the halfway point, where the molecule is completely flat, is the hardest part of the journey.

The two molecules in the paper make a useful pair. Hydronium is a water molecule that has picked up an extra proton. It is positively charged, it is flatter than ammonia (the H–O–H angle is about 112°, against about 107° in ammonia), and it flips easily. Phosphine is ammonia with the nitrogen swapped for phosphorus, the next element down the same column of the periodic table. Its bonds are longer, and its H–P–H angle is only about 93°, so it is a tall, narrow pyramid, and it almost never flips. The reason the angles differ so much is a story about how much the phosphorus 3s and 3p orbitals mix, which I will leave aside here; what matters for us is that one of these molecules sits near the easy end of inversion, and the other near the hard end.

Two valleys and a hill

To say anything quantitative, we need to talk about energy. Picture a line along which the molecule flips, from “pyramid pointing up”, through “flat”, to “pyramid pointing down”, and plot the molecule’s energy at each point along it. The two pyramids are equally comfortable, so they sit at the bottoms of two identical valleys. The flat shape is strained, so it sits at the top of a hill between them. Chemists call this a double-well potential, the top of the hill is the transition state, and the height of the hill above the valley floor is the inversion barrier.

The horizontal axis needs a name, and the paper calls it the reaction coordinate. Informally, it measures how far the molecule is from flat, and which way it is pointing. (Formally, it is a “mass-weighted” distance, measured in units of bohr·amu½, which takes into account that it is mostly the light hydrogens that move. You can ignore the units and think of it as “umbrella-ness”.)

A detour on units

Spectroscopists measure energies in wavenumbers, cm⁻¹, which looks strange for an energy. The idea is that light of a given energy has a given wavelength, and the wavenumber is just how many of those wavelengths fit into a centimetre, so higher wavenumber means higher energy. Some conversions to hold on to: 1 kcal/mol is about 350 cm⁻¹, and the typical thermal energy available to a molecule at room temperature, kBT, is about 208 cm⁻¹.

On that scale, the hydronium barrier of about 700 cm⁻¹ is only about three and a half times the thermal energy, and the phosphine barrier of about 11,600 cm⁻¹ is more than fifty times it.

If molecules behaved like balls rolling on a landscape, the story would end here. A ball with less energy than the hill would roll back and forth inside one valley forever. A ball with more would roll over the top. The barrier would be a wall, and only molecules that were hot enough would ever flip.

Going through the hill

Molecules are not balls, though, and at this scale the rules are quantum mechanical. Two things change.

The first is that a molecule cannot have any energy it likes. Confined to a valley, it can only have certain energies, the energy levels, and it can never sit perfectly still at the bottom: even the lowest level sits some way above the valley floor (this leftover energy is called the zero-point energy). Each level comes with a wavefunction, ψ, whose square tells you how likely you are to find the molecule at each point along the reaction coordinate.

The second change is the one that matters for inversion. A wavefunction does not stop dead at the edge of a valley. It leaks into the hill, fading away exponentially, and if the hill is thin enough and low enough, a little of it reaches the other side. So the molecule does not have to climb over the barrier to get to the other valley; there is a probability that it is simply found on the other side. This is quantum tunnelling.

One consequence is beautiful and is what you can actually measure. Because the two valleys are identical, the wavefunctions have to be either symmetric (the same on both sides, labelled +) or antisymmetric (equal and opposite, labelled −). Without tunnelling, those two would have exactly the same energy. With tunnelling, they are split apart by a small amount, the tunnelling splitting, ΔE, and each level becomes a closely spaced pair, a doublet. Friedrich Hund worked out this picture in 1927 , and it was soon used to explain a doubling of lines in ammonia’s spectrum . Ammonia’s ground-state splitting is about 0.79 cm⁻¹, which corresponds to a microwave frequency of about 23.8 GHz, and that is where the opening line of this post comes from. One of ammonia’s inversion lines near that frequency is also what the first maser, built in 1954, ran on .

The splitting is extraordinarily sensitive to the shape of the barrier. Make the hill a little higher or a little wider, and the splitting does not shrink a little; it shrinks exponentially. That sensitivity is why inversion is a good probe of the environment a molecule is in, and it is the thing to play with below.

There is another way to see what a splitting means. If you could prepare the molecule so that it is definitely in the left valley, that state is not one of the energy levels but a mixture of the + and − states of a pair. Left alone, the mixture does not stay put: it sloshes into the right valley and back again, and the time it takes to go there and back is set by the splitting, T = h/ΔE. A large splitting means fast sloshing, and a tiny splitting means the molecule stays where it is for a very long time.

For hydronium the back-and-forth takes well under a picosecond. For phosphine, which has a much higher and wider barrier, the calculated splitting is so small (well below 10⁻¹¹ cm⁻¹, with estimates that span several orders of magnitude depending on how you compute it) that the round trip would take anywhere from seconds to about a day, which on a molecular timescale is close to forever. No inversion splitting has ever been seen in phosphine’s spectrum, although full-dimensional calculations suggest it might show up in highly excited bending states . One of our molecules is a fast tunneller, and the other is, for practical purposes, stuck.

A cage made of carbon

C₆₀ is a hollow ball of sixty carbon atoms, arranged in twelve pentagons and twenty hexagons exactly like the panels of a football. It was discovered in 1985 , and its carbon atoms sit on a sphere about 7 Å across. Once you allow for the size of the carbon atoms’ own electron clouds, that leaves an empty space in the middle only about 3.7 Å across, and chemists have found ways to put things in it. Molecules inside fullerenes are called endohedral, and they are written with an @ sign, so a water molecule inside C₆₀ is H₂O@C₆₀.

This is not only a thought experiment. Using a sequence of reactions sometimes called “molecular surgery”, chemists open a hole in the cage, slip a molecule in, and stitch the hole closed again. Hydrogen was put inside C₆₀ in 2005 , and water in 2011 , and once inside, these molecules keep rotating and vibrating while held away from everything else. They have become a kind of laboratory for studying a single molecule in a very clean, very small box.

That raises a question. If tunnelling is so sensitive to the shape of the barrier, what does the box do to it? Physicists have known since the 1940s that squeezing a quantum oscillator into a box pushes its energy levels up , but a flip is a more delicate thing than a single vibration. Does squeezing a molecule make it harder to flip, because there is less room, or easier, because of how the cage pulls on it? Is the answer the same for a charged molecule and a neutral one? Our group had already looked at ammonia inside C₆₀ , and this paper asks the same questions for hydronium and phosphine.

To answer the question, though, we have to be able to calculate the double well for a molecule that is surrounded by sixty carbon atoms. That needs a detour into how molecules are calculated at all.

How do you calculate a molecule?

Everything about a molecule, its shape, its energy, how it vibrates, follows in principle from one equation, the Schrödinger equation. The trouble is in the words “in principle”.

The first simplification is the Born–Oppenheimer approximation. Nuclei are thousands of times heavier than electrons, so the electrons rearrange themselves almost instantly whenever the nuclei move. That means you can freeze the nuclei in place, solve for the electrons, and get an energy for that one arrangement of nuclei. Do that for many arrangements and you get a potential energy surface, and the double well from the last section is a slice through exactly such a surface.

So the real problem is the electrons. The difficulty is that the electrons all repel each other, so the position of every electron depends on where all the others are, and the wavefunction that describes them is a function of all their coordinates at once: three coordinates per electron. Hydronium has 10 electrons, so its wavefunction is a function of 30 variables. C₆₀ has 360 electrons, so its wavefunction lives in 1,080 dimensions. You cannot store such a thing, let alone solve for it directly.

Every practical method in quantum chemistry is a way of approximating this problem, and they trade accuracy for cost in different ways. Two families matter for this paper.

Hartree–Fock, and what it leaves out

The oldest approach is the Hartree–Fock method. Instead of letting every electron respond to every other electron individually, it lets each electron move in the average field of all the others. Each electron then gets its own wavefunction, an orbital, and these are the orbitals you meet in chemistry classes. The catch is that the average field depends on the orbitals, and the orbitals depend on the field, so the method goes round in a loop: guess the orbitals, build the field, solve for new orbitals, rebuild the field, and repeat until nothing changes. This loop is called the self-consistent field (SCF), and DFT uses the same idea.

What Hartree–Fock leaves out is that real electrons dodge each other on the fly, rather than just feeling an average. The energy that comes from this dodging is called the correlation energy. It is a small fraction of the total, but chemistry happens in small differences, so it matters a great deal. One part of it matters for this paper in particular: dispersion, the weak, attractive “London” force that arises when the electrons of two neighbouring molecules fluctuate in step with each other. It is why noble gases liquefy at all, and Hartree–Fock does not capture it.

Methods that add correlation back on top of Hartree–Fock are called post-Hartree–Fock, or wavefunction methods. MP2 adds it as a correction using perturbation theory. Coupled cluster goes much further, and the version known as CCSD(T), which treats single and double excitations of electrons in full and adds triple excitations approximately , is often called the “gold standard” of quantum chemistry, because for well-behaved molecules, with a large enough basis set, it gets energies right to within about a kilocalorie per mole. It is also very expensive. Its cost grows roughly as the seventh power of the size of the system, so doubling the size of a molecule makes the calculation about a hundred and twenty-eight times slower.

Density functional theory

Density functional theory (DFT) comes at the problem from the other end. In 1964, Hohenberg and Kohn proved something surprising: the ground-state energy of a system of electrons is completely determined by its electron density, the three-dimensional function from the figure above . You do not need the 3N-dimensional wavefunction to get the energy, in principle; the density, which is a function of only three coordinates, contains all the information.

The catch is that the proof says such a mapping from density to energy, a functional, exists, but not what it is. A year later, Kohn and Sham found a practical route . They imagined a fictitious system of electrons that do not interact with each other but have exactly the same density as the real ones. For non-interacting electrons, almost everything can be calculated exactly, and all the difficult many-body physics gets pushed into one leftover term, the exchange–correlation functional. If we knew that term exactly, DFT would be exact. We do not, and the hundreds of “functionals” in use today, with names like B3LYP, PBE0, M06-2X and B97-D, are different approximations to it. John Perdew described them as rungs on a “Jacob’s ladder”, climbing from simple approximations towards the exact answer, with each rung costing more .

In practice, DFT costs roughly as much as Hartree–Fock but includes a good part of the correlation energy, which is why it is the workhorse of computational chemistry. Its weaknesses are that there is no systematic way to improve a given functional, so you have to check how a functional does on problems similar to yours, and that most functionals miss dispersion too. They include correlation, but they work out the energy by looking at the density at and near each point, while dispersion is a correlation between electrons that are far apart. Stefan Grimme’s fix was pragmatic: add a simple, empirically fitted attraction between every pair of atoms that falls off as 1/r⁶, the way dispersion does. The functional we ended up using, B97-D, is one he built with that correction included from the start . For a molecule sitting inside a cage of sixty carbon atoms, dispersion is not a detail.

Basis sets

There is one more ingredient, and it is the part of a method’s name after the slash. Orbitals are smooth functions in three-dimensional space, and computers work with finite lists of numbers, so every calculation builds its orbitals out of a fixed set of simpler functions, a basis set, and only solves for how much of each to mix in.

The natural building blocks would be functions shaped like the orbitals of the hydrogen atom, which fall off as e−r. But the integrals that a calculation needs are much faster to compute with Gaussian functions, e−αr², so almost all of quantum chemistry builds its orbitals out of sums of Gaussians. A single Gaussian is the wrong shape: it is too flat at the nucleus, where the true orbital has a sharp point, and it dies away too quickly far from it. Add a few with different widths, and the sum gets close.

The basis sets in this paper have names like aug-cc-pVTZ, which unpacks as follows. cc-p means “correlation-consistent polarised”, a family designed by Thom Dunning so that results improve systematically as the sets get bigger . VTZ means valence triple-zeta: each valence orbital gets three functions of different sizes, so it can stretch or contract as the bonding demands. Polarised means there are also functions of higher angular momentum (d and f functions on a carbon atom, say) so that orbitals can bend and distort. And aug means augmented with very spread-out “diffuse” functions , which matter for ions, for weak interactions, and for the outer, loosely held parts of a molecule’s electron cloud. QZ, quadruple-zeta, is the next size up, and the larger the basis, the closer you get to the answer the method would give with a perfect basis, and the more it costs.

Why the cage needed DFT

Now the practical problem is clear. A free hydronium ion in the aug-cc-pVTZ basis is a small calculation. Put it inside C₆₀ and you add sixty carbon atoms, each of which brings its own set of basis functions, and the calculation is more than twenty times bigger. For a method whose cost grows as the seventh power of size, that is not a factor of twenty; it is a factor of billions.

So the paper splits the work. For the free molecules, which are small, we computed CCSD(T) energies with the large aug-cc-pVQZ basis along the path, to get the most reliable double wells we could, and compared them against experiment where experiment exists. For the caged molecules, the full double well had to come from DFT. And to check the strength of the binding between the guest and the cage, which needs high accuracy at only a few geometries, we used DLPNO-CCSD(T), a local approximation to coupled cluster developed in Frank Neese’s group, the group behind ORCA , which makes coupled-cluster-quality energies possible for systems the size of a fullerene.

Choosing a functional

Which DFT functional, then? This is where one has to be careful. In our earlier work on ammonia inside C₆₀, the M06-2X functional had reproduced the experimental inversion barrier well , so the obvious move would have been to use it again. Before trusting any functional, though, we tested several of them against CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVQZ on the free molecules, where both could be computed.

For phosphine, almost everything gets the barrier right to within about 7%. For hydronium, the methods are all over the place, and M06-2X, which had done so well for ammonia, gives a barrier a third to a half too low, depending on the basis set. B97-D with the aug-cc-pVTZ basis was the only functional that did well on both molecules, so that is what we used for the caged systems. It is still about 13% low for hydronium (612 against 706 cm⁻¹), which is worth remembering when we get to the results.

I find this one of the more useful lessons of the project, and it is the one I would pass on to anyone starting out the way I did. There is no “best functional”. There is the functional that has been shown to work for your kind of problem, and the only way to know is to check.

Tracing the path

With the method chosen, the calculation of a double well goes through a few steps, each of which is a standard job type in a program like ORCA or Gaussian.

First, geometry optimisation: start from a rough guess of the pyramid and let the program move the atoms downhill until the forces on them vanish. That gives the bottom of a valley. Second, find the transition state, the flat geometry at the top of the hill. A transition state is a saddle point: it is a maximum along the reaction coordinate and a minimum in every other direction. A frequency calculation confirms which is which, because a true minimum has only real vibrational frequencies, while a transition state has exactly one imaginary frequency, whose motion is the flip itself. The barrier height is then just the difference in energy between the two.

Third, the path between them. An intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) calculation starts at the transition state and follows the steepest way down, in mass-weighted coordinates, until it reaches the valley . That gives one half of the double well, from the top of the hill to the bottom of the valley. But the wavefunctions also spread up the far wall of each valley, the side where the pyramid is squashed taller than its equilibrium shape, so we ran a second set of IRC calculations starting from compressed pyramids and following them back down. Joining the two pieces, and using the fact that the two valleys are mirror images, gives the whole double well.

Fourth, a smooth curve through the points. The paper fits each double well to the form

$$V(x) = A x^4 + B\, e^{-C x^2} - D x^2,$$

a quartic wall that keeps the molecule from flying apart, a Gaussian bump for the barrier in the middle, and an inverted parabola that deepens the two valleys. (The paper writes the last term as +Dx² with a negative D; I have written the minus sign explicitly.) The constant B is the energy of the flat geometry, x = 0, and it equals the barrier height when the valley floors sit at zero.

Finally, the quantum part. With V(x) in hand, the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation for motion along x can be solved numerically for the energy levels and wavefunctions, which the paper does with the shooting method. This is exactly the calculation the playground earlier in this post is running in your browser, and solving it with the fitted parameters from the paper reproduces the paper’s lowest energy levels to within a few cm⁻¹, and the higher ones to within about half a per cent.

What the cage does

Here is the main result, with the double wells for both molecules, free and caged.

Hydronium gets stuck. Inside C₆₀, the B97-D barrier for hydronium rises from 612 to about 870 cm⁻¹, and the two valleys move further apart (the pyramid gets about 25% taller). Both changes make tunnelling harder, and the ground-state splitting falls from 104 to 38 cm⁻¹, a drop by almost two-thirds. For the free molecule, B97-D overestimates the splitting compared with experiment (104 against 55 cm⁻¹), while CCSD(T) gets much closer (49 to 65 cm⁻¹ depending on the basis set), so the absolute numbers for the caged molecule should not be taken too literally. The direction and the rough size of the effect, though, are what DFT should get right, since the same method is being compared with itself.

Why would the valleys move apart? Our interpretation in the paper is that it comes from the charge. Hydronium is a cation, and its positive charge pulls the electron cloud of the cage towards it, inducing a negative charge on the inner surface of the C₆₀. The ion is then attracted to that induced charge, and the attraction favours the pyramidal shapes over the flat one. That is an interpretation, and the paper does not test it separately.

Phosphine barely notices. Phosphine’s barrier was already enormous, and confinement lowers it only slightly, from about 11,600 to 11,000 cm⁻¹. It is still more than fifty times room-temperature thermal energy, and tunnelling stays negligible inside the cage as well as outside it. What changes is mostly the shape of the well: phosphine’s umbrella vibration shifts up a little (1027 to 1056 cm⁻¹), and the spacing between its energy levels grows slightly, which is what you would expect if the walls of the well get a little steeper.

So the same cage does opposite things to the two molecules. For the charged, floppy hydronium, it raises the barrier and suppresses tunnelling. For the neutral, rigid phosphine, it lowers the barrier slightly and otherwise changes very little.

The geometries and vibrations tell the same story. In the cage, hydronium’s O–H bonds stretch slightly (0.982 to 0.995 Å) and their stretching vibrations shift to lower frequencies, while the bending motion that drives the flip stiffens (842 to 1037 cm⁻¹). Phosphine’s P–H bonds shorten (1.428 to 1.396 Å) and all of its vibrations shift to higher frequencies, which is what you would expect of a molecule that is being pressed on from all sides. The cage itself barely moves: the carbon atoms shift by only about 0.07 Å (root-mean-square) when a guest is inside.

What holds them in

Is the molecule actually stable in there, or would it rather be outside? The interaction energy answers that: the energy of the guest inside the cage, minus the energies of the guest and the empty cage apart. A negative number means the combination is more stable than the two pieces.

With DLPNO-CCSD(T), the interaction energy is −30.8 kcal/mol for hydronium and −13.4 kcal/mol for phosphine . Both are bound, hydronium much more strongly. (B97-D gets hydronium about right, but underestimates phosphine’s binding by nearly a factor of two, which is a useful caution about using one method for everything.)

To see why they are bound, we split the interaction energy into physically meaningful pieces using the local energy decomposition (LED) built into ORCA . It is easiest to read as a budget.

Both molecules have to pay a large up-front cost, the electronic preparation energy, to squeeze their electron clouds into the space and to let the cage’s electrons rearrange around them. That cost is larger for phosphine (174.5 against 117.8 kcal/mol), because phosphine is the bigger molecule. They pay it back in different ways. Hydronium is held mostly by electrostatics, which makes sense for a positive ion surrounded by a polarisable cloud of 360 electrons. Phosphine gets a larger share of its binding from dispersion (38.9 against 18.3 kcal/mol), along with exchange and polarisation, the soft, correlated attraction that Hartree–Fock misses and that Grimme’s correction was designed to add back.

What this does not tell us

It is worth being plain about the limits of all this.

The double wells are one-dimensional. A real molecule has many ways to vibrate, and the umbrella motion is coupled to the others; for free hydronium, full-dimensional calculations have shown that the coupling is strong . Reducing inversion to a single coordinate captures the essentials, but the numbers it gives are those of a model.

The caged results come from DFT, and the free-molecule benchmarks show that B97-D underestimates hydronium’s barrier and overestimates its splitting. The comparison between free and caged is made with the same method on both sides, which is why I trust the direction of the effects more than their exact sizes, but I cannot rule out that the method’s errors behave differently inside the cage.

The phosphine splittings are so small that they sit at the edge of what these calculations can resolve. The paper itself points out that the computed values depend strongly on the method and that tiny numerical noise along the flat part of the potential can be amplified when the curve is interpolated. I would read the phosphine splittings as “negligible, free or caged”, and not put weight on any single number.

And these are calculations on idealised systems. As far as I know, neither OH₃⁺@C₆₀ nor PH₃@C₆₀ has been made in a laboratory (even ammonia inside C₆₀ was still described as a target in 2022), and a real sample of a caged cation would also have a counter-ion somewhere nearby, which our model does not include. So the predictions here are waiting for an experiment, and I would be curious to see whether the suppression of hydronium’s tunnelling shows up in a spectrum.

Coming back to it

What I find satisfying about this problem is how much of physical chemistry it touches with so few atoms. A four-atom molecule and a ball of carbon are enough to bring in potential energy surfaces, tunnelling, the particle in a box, the whole ladder of electronic structure methods, and the question of where binding comes from, and the answers are not the same for two molecules that look almost alike on paper.

It also raises questions I do not know the answers to. If a charged guest polarises the cage and that changes its barrier, could you tune a guest’s tunnelling by changing the cage, say with a larger fullerene, or one with a metal atom or a different charge? Would an external electric field, pushing on the induced charge, do something similar? And how well does the one-dimensional picture hold up once the cage is allowed to vibrate along with the guest?

Behind every number in this post is a lot of practical work that does not appear in the paper: input files, convergence failures, jobs that ran for days on a cluster and then had to be run again. I learned most of that by doing it badly first, and I want to write it up properly, which is what the next post will be about.
entry.summary: Some small molecules turn themselves inside out like an umbrella in the wind, and quantum mechanics lets them do it through a wall of energy they cannot climb. A visual walk through my paper on what happens to that flip when the molecule is shut inside a C₆₀ football, and an introduction to how chemists calculate any of this, density functional theory included.

entry.title: The quiet injury
entry.content:
Somewhere in the world, about once or twice every second, a force from outside the body changes how somebody’s brain works. Most of those people are told the injury is mild, and many walk out of the emergency department with a normal scan. For a good number of them, that is not the end of it.
0 people have had a traumatic brain injury since you opened this page, going by the lowest of the global estimates. The highest would make it about two and a half times as many.
Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

In 2023, for my undergraduate capstone at Krea University, I spent a few months with a US database of people who had had a traumatic brain injury. I wanted to know which other illnesses tended to turn up together in the years afterwards. The project was supervised by Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar. It led to a paper on how common those illnesses were five years after a mild injury , a perspective on why graph theory might help , and a paper on the networks they form . This series explains that work to someone who has never studied medicine, statistics or graph theory, which, at the start, was more or less me.

First, though, I need you to care about the injury. This part covers what happens inside a struck head, why “mild” misleads, and why researchers now treat TBI as a disease that lasts years. Part 2 builds the graph-theory toolkit, and Part 3 puts the two together.

An ordinary injury

By the consensus definition, a traumatic brain injury (TBI) is “an alteration in brain function, or other evidence of brain pathology, caused by an external force” . The force can be a blow, a fall, a sudden stop, a blast or a penetrating object. The result can be anything from a few minutes of confusion to a coma.

How many people does this happen to? Nobody knows to within a factor of two or so. The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study estimated 27.08 million new cases in 2016 . The Lancet Neurology Commission on TBI puts it at 50 to 60 million a year, and points out the gap itself . A third estimate, built from different studies, comes to 69 million .

Much of the spread comes from mild injury, which is most injury and often never reaches a hospital. The WHO task force on mild TBI put the hospital-treated rate at about 100 to 300 per 100,000 people a year, and the true rate at “probably above 600/100,000” . More than 90 per cent of all cases are classified as mild . So a number for TBI is mostly a number for mild TBI, and probably an undercount.

One self-reported estimate puts lifetime prevalence at up to 40% of adults . I find that hard to square with how rarely anyone mentions having had one. I suspect much of it is the kind of thing people describe as “I hit my head” and then stop thinking about.

Who gets hurt depends on where people live and how old they are. In high-income countries most TBI comes from falls, “particularly in older people (aged ≥65 years), who often have comorbidities” . In the United States, rates were highest in people aged 75 and over . In low- and middle-income countries road traffic dominates, “particularly those involving motorcyclists” .

India deserves its own paragraph, partly because I live here and partly because the numbers are so thin. The most-cited estimate is still from 2002: “nearly 1.5 to 2 million persons are injured” every year, mostly on the roads . That a twenty-year-old figure is still the reference point is itself a finding. A 2017 review of 72 Indian hospital studies found a mean in-hospital mortality of 24.6%, and judged the quality of reporting low .

What happens after the injury differs just as much. This is the starkest comparison I came across while reading for this series.

Hold on to the second pair: the database my project used is made up entirely of people discharged to inpatient rehabilitation in the United States. In India, that would describe almost nobody.

A soft thing in a hard box

Why can a blow that leaves the skull intact still hurt the brain? Partly because the brain is very soft. Its shear modulus (how easily one layer slides over another) is about 0.4 to 1.4 kilopascals . That is hard to feel, so the usual comparison is soft tofu or a set jelly, which holds its shape on a plate and tears if you pull it.

The brain floats in cerebrospinal fluid, tethered at the bottom by the brainstem and loosely by membranes and blood vessels. The skull is smooth outside, but the inside of its floor is not. The front of the brain rests on the bony roofs of the eye sockets. The tips of the temporal lobes sit in cup-shaped hollows behind a sharp ledge of bone, the sphenoid ridge. As Bigler puts it, these features “are uniquely situated to facilitate injury” to both places . Keep them in mind: the underside of the frontal lobes and the front tips of the temporal lobes.

The model below is a real brain surface, reconstructed from MRI. Turn it, open the skull, and pick a region.

The brain does not divide its work neatly, but roughly, the frontal lobes, especially their underside, are heavily involved in planning, holding back impulses and regulating emotion. The temporal lobes hold the machinery for forming new memories and processing emotion. Both sit on the rough parts of the skull floor. If you were designing a skull to protect personality, mood and memory, you would not put them there.

What a blow does

Now strike the box. The skull moves, and for an instant the loosely held brain stays where it was. The skull’s inner wall catches up and compresses it on the struck side. When the skull stops, the brain carries on and meets the far wall. The bruise at the site of the blow is called a coup injury, and the one opposite a contrecoup injury. Most non-penetrating injury comes from “rapid acceleration or deceleration of the head, with or without impact” . The motion is what hurts the brain, and the skull does not need to break.

Below is a deliberately crude model, a soft body in fluid inside a rigid shell with a ridged floor at the front. It is not a simulation of a brain, but it obeys the same rule: a soft, loosely held thing lags behind its container.

Try the blow to the forehead and the fall backwards. In both, the front of the body hits the front of the shell, once as coup and once as contrecoup. In a real head, each throw forwards or back also scrapes the front of the brain across the ridged floor. That is the intuition for why contusions cluster in the frontal and temporal poles more or less wherever the blow lands .

The 3D model does the same on real anatomy.

When the head turns

Surface bruises are only half the story, and for mild injury probably the smaller half. In 1943 the physicist A. H. S. Holbourn argued that brain tissue is very hard to compress but very easy to shear, so rotation damages it more than straight-line motion does . Twist a plate of jelly quickly and the edge goes with the plate while the middle lags, stretching the jelly in between. Ommaya and Gennarelli later proposed that harder rotation shears progressively deeper structures .

The evidence is from monkeys, unpleasant to read but clear. In 1982 Gennarelli and colleagues rotated the heads of 45 primates without any impact, varying only the direction. Front-to-back rotation mostly caused a brief coma, and every concussed animal recovered. Sideways rotation left 20 animals in coma for more than six hours, with the axonal damage seen in severe human injury. The authors concluded that “axonal damage produced by coronal head acceleration is a major cause of prolonged traumatic coma and its sequelae” . Nothing had struck any of those skulls.

How hard is the motion in an ordinary concussion? The best numbers come from American football, where impacts can be filmed, reconstructed or recorded by helmet sensors.

A concussed professional player’s head took, on average, about 98 times the acceleration of gravity for about 15 milliseconds . What I find more telling is the overlap. Concussive impacts in college players ranged from about 61 g to 169 g, and clinical severity had nothing to do with impact size . The same blow can concuss one person and not the next.

What rotation does inside is easiest to picture with the brain’s wiring. Nerve cells talk over long, thin cables called axons, bundled together in the white matter. Each is held in shape by protein tubes (microtubules) that double as transport rails. Axons are “especially vulnerable to injury due to the mechanical loading of the brain”. Diffuse damage to them “may represent a key pathologic substrate of mild TBI (concussion)” .

The stretch lasts milliseconds, but the damage plays out over a day. In people, “axonal degeneration has been found to continue even years after injury” . Nor is it randomly placed. In 434 fatal head injuries, Adams and colleagues graded diffuse axonal injury by how deep it reached. The mildest grade involved the white matter of the hemispheres, the next the corpus callosum (the band joining the two halves), and the worst the upper brainstem .

None of this needs a broken skull, a bleed, or anything visible on the CT scan used in most emergency departments. In one study of 135 people with mild TBI, 27% of those with a normal CT had an abnormal MRI soon after. Some of those MRI findings predicted a worse outcome at three months . A normal CT does not show that the brain was spared.

Some of this damage can be seen in living people, though only on average, by watching water. Inside a bundle of axons, water drifts far more easily along the fibres than across them. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures that preference in every small cube of the brain . It summarises it as fractional anisotropy (FA), from 0 if water spreads equally every way to near 1 if only along a line . Following the preferred direction from cube to cube traces the bundles themselves.

The intuition is that a damaged axon should leak, making diffusion less directional and FA lower. In group studies that is broadly what turns up, most consistently in the corpus callosum and the frontal tracts . Then again, the differences are small and shift with time. Some studies in the first two weeks find FA higher than normal, and later ones mostly find it lower . This is also how a CT can be normal while DTI is not. CT shows blood and broken bone, and a stretched axon contains neither.

All of this describes groups, and I want to be plain about that. In the TRACK-TBI study, patients whose CT and MRI were clear showed no significant DTI difference from controls as a group . The radiologists’ review concluded that DTI belongs, for now, to research comparisons, and cannot yet tell whether one particular person’s white matter was injured . What the figure shows is where group studies have looked and found differences.

The second injury

Everything so far happens in the first fraction of a second. This primary injury is “the direct mechanical damage”, which “cannot be therapeutically influenced” . What follows over hours, days and weeks is the secondary injury, and that is where medicine has tried to intervene.

Giza and Hovda pulled decades of animal work together into what they called the neurometabolic cascade of concussion . It explains why a brain that looks fine can be unusually fragile for a while.

The figure’s stages give the detail. In short, ions flood across damaged membranes, and the cells burn through their energy putting them back. A long slump follows, “a state of impaired metabolism that can last up to 7-10 days in adult animals” .

Everyone who plays a contact sport should know that during this slump, the brain is more vulnerable to a second injury. Clinically, the riskiest window looks like the first ten days. In animals, two injuries three to five days apart did more damage than two injuries seven days apart . Inflammation adds another layer, and it has been linked to later neurodegeneration .

Why there is no drug

If the secondary injury unfolds over days, you would think it could be interrupted, and people have tried for decades. Our BMC Neurology paper says it flatly: “no drug exists to prevent the spread of secondary injuries after a primary impact” . That sentence is backed by an unusual amount of failure.

A 2010 review counted 33 large phase III trials in TBI between 1980 and 2009, with “disappointing results” . Steroids made things worse . Progesterone failed twice: ProTECT III was stopped for futility , and SyNAPSe found no difference . Donald Stein, who had championed progesterone, wrote afterwards that “a 100% failure rate continues to plague the field of TBI trials” . Dr Sudhakar’s own review found that drugs acting on the brain’s main inhibitory signalling system “fail to produce any neuroprotection after a primary impact to the brain” in animal models .

I should be precise, because the claim is easy to overstate. Neurosurgery, intensive care and rehabilitation do help people with TBI. One drug, tranexamic acid, reduced head-injury deaths in mild to moderate TBI when given within three hours, though it works by stopping bleeding rather than by protecting nerve cells . What has not worked, so far, is a drug that protects brain cells from the secondary cascade. Why is argued about, and I am not in a position to settle it. Many of the explanations come back to one point, though, which is that TBI is not one disease. The mix of bruising, bleeding, axonal damage and swelling differs from person to person, and so does what comes after.

Counting consciousness

The most widely used measure of severity is the Glasgow Coma Scale, published by Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett in 1974 . It scores how readily a person’s eyes open, how well they talk, and how well they move on command, for a total between 3 and 15. My project and both papers sorted people by the total at admission into mild (13 to 15), moderate (9 to 12) and severe (3 to 8) . Try it.

Play with it and something odd shows up. Eyes opening to speech, confused talk and obeying commands give 3 + 4 + 6 = 13, which is mild. Eyes open spontaneously, orientated talk, but only localising to pressure give 4 + 5 + 5 = 14, also mild, and milder. Very different people land on the same total. Forty years on, Teasdale himself wrote that “individual patients are best described by the three components of the coma scale; whereas the derived total coma score should be used to characterise groups” . That caveat applies to my own work, which used a single total taken at admission.

Mild is not minor

“Mild” describes the score in the first hours, not the consequences. A textbook chapter warns that “for a sizeable minority of patients diagnosed with mTBI, the term can seem a cruel misnomer”. Most people’s symptoms (headache, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, low mood and others) subside within three months. But “in up to 30% of patients with mTBI, they can persist well beyond 6 months” .

Large studies have since found it worse than that. TRACK-TBI followed 1,154 people with mild TBI from eleven US trauma centres, with 299 orthopaedic patients for comparison . Its outcome measure, the Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended, scores 8 for a full return to life as before. Anything lower means some injury-related limitation.

At two weeks, 87% of the mild TBI group reported some limitation. At twelve months 53% still did, against 38% of the orthopaedic patients . The comparison group answers the obvious objection. Any injury bad enough for a trauma centre is disruptive, so some of that 53% has nothing to do with the brain, but the excess is harder to explain away. At three and six months, about a fifth of the mild TBI group had probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or major depression. In the orthopaedic group it was roughly a tenth . In Europe, CENTER-TBI found that 30% of people sent home from the emergency department had not fully recovered at six months .

Yet in CENTER-TBI only 26% were given written information, and 6% a follow-up appointment . The blunt labels cut the other way too. In TRACK-TBI, 52.4% of people with severe TBI and 75% with moderate TBI had a favourable outcome by twelve months . The label given at admission is a rough guide to what follows, in both directions.

A process, not an event

In 2010 Brent Masel and Douglas DeWitt published a paper whose title is the argument: “Traumatic brain injury: a disease process, not an event”. They argued that TBI “increases long-term mortality and reduces life expectancy”, and linked it to illnesses in and beyond the brain. Their aim was not to discourage patients, “but rather to emphasize that TBI should be managed as a chronic disease” . Outcomes can improve or worsen “up to two decades after injury” , and between one and five years, “decline occurs as frequently as improvement” .

The timeline below gathers some of the evidence. It is not one person’s story, and the studies do not follow the same people.

In 2.79 million Danes, any TBI carried about 1.24 times the risk of dementia, rising with the number of injuries . In Denmark, too, the suicide rate was about 1.8 times as high after mild TBI alone . A US study followed 4,351 people with mild TBI and 4,351 matched controls for up to ten years. Mild TBI carried about 2.5 times the risk of high blood pressure, and 5.9 times in people aged 18 to 40. New conditions appeared at a median of three and a half years . In the US database I used, life expectancy was about nine years shorter than in comparable people .

Some of these associations will be causal and some will not. People who fall over, or crash motorbikes, are not a random sample of people. Existing conditions can make an injury more likely, and the same habits or circumstances can raise the risk of both. Studies adjust for what they can, but none can adjust for everything. That applies to my own work too, as Part 3 discusses.

Illnesses that travel together

The word for what that timeline is circling is comorbidity. It means two or more conditions in the same person, together or one after the other. By itself, it says nothing about why. Two neighbouring words do claim a cause. A complication is something the injury or its treatment directly brings about, usually soon after (a seizure in the first week). A sequela is a lasting consequence of the injury (memory problems from a damaged temporal lobe). Comorbidity is the agnostic term, and the honest one for survey data like mine, which shows that two conditions go together but not how.

Why do conditions go together? I found this the most interesting question in the project, and it is the one my data could answer least. There are at least six routes, and they leave very similar footprints.

The first is chance, since two common conditions will often coincide. The second is causation, as when chronic pain leads to depression. The third is a shared mechanism, such as damage to emotional circuits producing both anxiety and low mood. The fourth is a shared risk factor, or confounder; age, for instance, raises the risk of high blood pressure and cataracts together. The fifth is treatment, where a medicine for one condition brings on another. The sixth is detection, because people already under a doctor’s care get examined and diagnosed more. My project could not tell these apart. Knowing they exist, though, changes how you read every line in a comorbidity network.

Here is what is known, and what is suspected, about the conditions that follow a brain injury.

Psychiatric

Anxiety, depression and PTSD were among the five commonest new conditions five years after mild TBI in the database I used . Probable PTSD or major depression was more than twice as common after mild TBI as after an orthopaedic injury at three months . Proposed routes include damage to the regions that regulate emotion and the upheaval any serious injury brings.

Substance use

Here the arrow often points the other way. Alcohol is involved in 15 to 20% of TBIs in India and contributed in a quarter of CENTER-TBI patients , so drinking is as much cause as consequence. Accidental poisoning is among the causes of death with the highest excess risk after TBI .

Heart, blood vessels and metabolism

After mild TBI, high blood pressure, diabetes and stroke all became more likely over the following decade, even in people aged 18 to 40 . Why is not settled. Metabolic dysregulation , reduced activity, poor sleep and stress are proposed routes rather than established ones.

Hormones

The hypothalamus and pituitary, which run most of the body’s hormone systems, sit just above the skull floor. Neuroendocrine dysregulation is a recognised long-term consequence , and injury to that region is the usual proposed route.

Neurological

Seizures, sleep disorders and neurodegenerative disease are all associated with TBI . Continuing axonal degeneration is one proposed link .

Pain and the body

Chronic pain was as common as depression five years after mild TBI , and back pain topped the list ten years after moderate and severe TBI . The accident that injures the brain often injures the body too.

None of these families sits in isolation. Pain disturbs sleep, poor sleep lowers mood, low mood makes it harder to stay active, and inactivity raises blood pressure. Each link is plausible, though nothing here shows that they operate after TBI. Still, a possible circle like that is the best reason I can give for treating these conditions as a network rather than a list.

Tangles

This is where my project begins. The first paper asked a simple question of the TBI Model Systems (TBIMS) database, the largest longitudinal TBI dataset in the world . Five years after a mild TBI, how many people had been diagnosed with each of 26 conditions since their injury ? Of 10,564 people with a recorded admission GCS, 4,915 (46.5%) were mild. One caveat runs through the series: these are not typical concussions. Everyone in TBIMS was admitted for inpatient rehabilitation, which fewer than one in ten hospitalised TBI patients receive . The mild cases typically had visible brain pathology or post-traumatic amnesia . Only 223 to 228 of them answered the questions about other conditions at five years; Part 3 explains why.

Of the 26, ten stand out by how common they were.

Anxiety (16.1%), depression (15.7%), chronic pain (15.7%), high blood pressure (14.0%) and PTSD (11.2%) top the list . Younger people had more depression, and older people more of the conditions that come with age. PTSD was more common in women. The paper concluded that people with mild TBI “could develop serious long-term medical and psychiatric comorbidities which could affect their pace of recovery” . It said nothing about cause, deliberately.

A list of percentages, though, treats each condition as if it lived alone. Someone with depression after a brain injury is also more likely to have anxiety, panic attacks and trouble sleeping. The button above shows that those overlaps are not small, and that once you draw the lines, the list turns into a tangle. My capstone was really about how to see the structure of a tangle like that. Which conditions sit at the centre, and which ones bridge otherwise separate groups? Does the shape change with age? Could a rare condition matter because of where it sits, rather than how often it occurs? And if so, what would a doctor do differently?

Answering those questions needs a way of thinking about connections that most people (and I, at the start of the project) have never been taught. That is what Part 2 is for.

Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

About the 3D brain: the cortex is FreeSurfer’s fsaverage surface (Fischl et al. 1999), parcellated with the Destrieux atlas (Destrieux et al. 2010); deep structures come from the Harvard-Oxford and Juelich atlases in MNI152 space, processed with nilearn (Abraham et al. 2014). The skull and fibre bundles are derived or stylised, and the mechanics are a toy model. Sources and build steps are in the repository’s assets/data/tbi/README.md.
entry.summary: Part 1 of a series on traumatic brain injury. What a brain injury is, how a blow that never breaks the skull can still damage a brain, why “mild” is a misleading word, and why the injury is better thought of as the start of a long process than as an event.

entry.title: Thinking in graphs
entry.content:
In 1735 Leonhard Euler settled a question about the bridges of a Prussian city by throwing away almost everything there was to know about the city.
Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

How do you look at a tangle?

Part 1 ended with the conditions that turn up in the years after a mild traumatic brain injury. Think of one person five years on. A scan might show nothing, but they are more likely to be living with depression, anxiety, poor sleep, chronic pain or high blood pressure, often several at once. Across thousands of people, each carries a different handful of conditions, and the handfuls overlap in ways that are hard to hold in your head. This post is about how you look at a tangle like that.

The answer I used in my undergraduate capstone at Krea University, supervised by Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar, and in the papers that followed , was graph theory. I had not met it formally before, and what follows is what I wish someone had shown me at the start. I think the ideas are much simpler than their notation suggests.

One move runs through the whole series. It is recasting: taking a problem that seems to be about a city, a group of friends or a population of patients, and deciding that only what is connected to what matters. Everything else is thrown away. Sometimes that is a real loss, but it is what lets one set of tools work on bridges, friendships, power grids, brains and diseases.

Seven bridges

Königsberg (now Kaliningrad) was built where the river Pregel splits around two islands, with seven bridges joining the islands and banks. The story goes that people liked to ask whether a walk could cross every bridge exactly once. Try it.

You will have got stuck, as everyone does, but six failures do not prove the seventh will fail. Euler showed that it must. His first step was to notice that the shape of the islands, the length of the bridges and the streets in between do not change the answer. All that matters is which land masses are joined by how many bridges. That is the recasting: each land mass becomes a dot and each bridge a line.

The second step is a short counting argument. Take any land mass that is neither the start nor the end of the walk. Every time you arrive by one bridge you must leave by another, so it must touch an even number of bridges. Only the start and the end can be odd. In Königsberg, Kneiphof touches five bridges and the other three land masses touch three each. Four odd land masses, and a walk has only two ends, so no route exists.

Building bridges in the figure lets you check the converse: with no odd land masses, or exactly two, a walk exists. Euler stated this, but the proof that the condition is enough came from Carl Hierholzer in 1873 , and “Find a walk” uses his method. The real city has since changed, and in 2006 the chemist Roger Mallion walked an Eulerian route through Kaliningrad . One correction to the usual story, though: Euler reasoned with letters, and the dots-and-lines drawings only appear in the late nineteenth century . The idea that only the connections matter is his.

Dots and lines

A graph $G = (V, E)$ is a set of nodes (or vertices) $V$ and a set of edges $E$, each joining two nodes. That is the whole definition. A graph is a guest list together with a list of who knows whom; it says nothing about where anyone is standing.

An edge can also carry a weight, saying how strong the connection is, or a direction, as a follow on social media does. The disease networks in Part 3 are weighted, because some pairs of conditions are much more strongly associated than others. They are undirected, because the study only sees two conditions turning up in the same people. That says nothing on its own about which, if either, led to the other, and an arrow would claim something the data cannot support.

The table is the adjacency matrix $A$: $a_{ij} = 1$ if nodes $i$ and $j$ are joined and $0$ if not, or the edge’s weight in a weighted graph. The formulas below use it. Now drag a few people around, or press “Redraw the picture”. The matrix does not change, because the graph has not. Where a node sits on the page carries no information unless someone decided that it should. It is tempting to read two nearby nodes in a paper’s figure as similar, but the data is the list of edges, and the layout is a choice made to help the eye.

Who has the most friends?

The first question anyone asks of a network is who has the most connections. The degree of a node $u$ is the number of edges touching it, the row sum of the adjacency matrix:

\[k_u = \sum_{v} a_{uv}.\]

In a weighted graph, the weighted degree, or strength, adds up the weights instead, where $w_{uv}$ is the weight of the edge between $u$ and $v$ (zero if there is none):

\[s_u = \sum_{v} w_{uv}.\]

Ravi has the most friends, but they are all acquaintances; Mina has fewer, and they are close. To know who hears gossip from the most directions, count. To know whose absence would be felt most, weigh. In a comorbidity network, a high degree means a condition is associated with many others, and a high weighted degree means its associations are strong. These need not be the same conditions.

The third button shows Scott Feld’s 1991 observation that most people have fewer friends than their friends do, on average . It follows from arithmetic alone. Popular people appear in many friends’ lists, so averaging over friends counts them again and again. The average over edges is $\langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle$, which exceeds the ordinary mean $\langle k \rangle$ whenever degrees vary. Anything found by following edges, patients or conditions, shows the same bias towards the well connected.

How much could be connected, and is?

Among $V$ nodes there are $V(V-1)/2$ possible pairs, and the density is the share of them that are joined by the $E$ edges:

\[\text{density} = \frac{2E}{V(V-1)}.\]

I think of the faint lines as ghosts, friendships that could exist and don’t. Possible pairs grow with the square of the number of nodes, so most real networks are very sparse: no one can know everyone in a city. A disease network has only a couple of dozen nodes, so its density can be much higher. In Part 3 the interesting question is which ghosts became real, and why those.

How far apart is everyone?

The distance $\delta(v_i, v_j)$ between two nodes is the number of edges on the shortest path between them. The method for finding it, breadth-first search, has a lovely physical picture. Drop a stone into a pond at the starting node. The first ripple reaches its neighbours, the second their neighbours, and the ripple that first touches a node tells you how far away it is.

The average path length is the mean distance over every pair,

\[\bar{\delta} = \frac{2}{V(V-1)} \sum_{i \lt j} \delta(v_i, v_j),\]

and the diameter $D = \max_{i,j} \delta(v_i, v_j)$ is the largest. In the histogram they are the dashed line and the right-most bar. Now press “Add a shortcut”. One edge between far corners pulls the whole histogram left, because it shortens every journey that can use it. Hold on to that for the small-world idea later.

The most famous path-length measurement was made with letters. In the 1960s Stanley Milgram and Jeffrey Travers asked 296 people to get a document to a Massachusetts stockbroker through first-name acquaintances. The 64 chains that arrived took an average of 5.2 intermediaries , the source of “six degrees of separation”. In 2012 the same quantity for Facebook’s roughly 721 million active users came out at 4.74 .

For diseases, a short path links two conditions through a few intermediates, each co-occurring with the next. It is easy to read such a path as a mechanism, one condition leading to the next. In an undirected co-occurrence network it is only a chain of associations, which suggests where to look but does not show what happens.

Are my friends friends with each other?

Pick a person and look only at their friends. Do those friends know each other? If node $u$ has $k_u$ neighbours, they could share $k_u(k_u-1)/2$ edges. If $E_u$ of those exist, the clustering coefficient is

\[C_u = \frac{2E_u}{k_u(k_u-1)}, \qquad 0 \le C_u \le 1.\]

Each edge between two neighbours closes a triangle through $u$, so $E_u$ also counts $u$’s triangles. The average clustering is the mean over all nodes, $\bar{C} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_u C_u$.

Clustering is density again, but local. A network can be sparse overall and still made of tight knots, as social networks usually are, because friends introduce their friends. A node with fewer than two neighbours has no pairs to close. networkx, the Python library the analysis used, scores it 0 and keeps it in the average , while Gephi leaves it out. For the network in my thesis these conventions give 0.38 and 0.42, and the thesis reported the second.

In a disease network, a triangle is three conditions where each pair co-occurs more than chance would predict. It cannot say whether the knot reflects a shared cause, a shared treatment or a shared way of being diagnosed, but it is a good place to start asking.

Do hubs hold hands?

Do well-connected nodes link to each other, or mostly to poorly connected ones? This is degree assortativity, and Mark Newman measured it directly . Take every edge, write down the degree at each end, and compute the correlation between the two columns:

\[r = \frac{\sum_{e} j_e k_e / M - \left[ \sum_{e} \tfrac{1}{2}(j_e + k_e) / M \right]^2}{\sum_{e} \tfrac{1}{2}(j_e^2 + k_e^2) / M - \left[ \sum_{e} \tfrac{1}{2}(j_e + k_e) / M \right]^2},\]

where $j_e$ and $k_e$ are the degrees at the two ends of edge $e$, over $M$ edges. It is just a Pearson correlation, from $-1$ (hubs attach to the periphery) to $+1$ (hubs attach to hubs).

The rewiring shows that assortativity belongs to the wiring, not the degrees. Every node keeps its number of edges, yet the hubs can be pushed from avoiding each other into a dense core. Newman found that social networks tend to be assortative, and technological and biological ones disassortative . In a disease network, positive assortativity would mean a core of highly comorbid conditions associated with each other. One caution I would give my undergraduate self: on a couple of dozen nodes, this coefficient rests on few edges and can swing if a handful change.

Who matters?

“Which node is most important?” has no single answer. There are several centralities, each making “important” precise in a different way, and my research used three. Degree centrality is the simplest: the degree, usually divided by $n-1$ so that a node connected to everyone scores 1.

Betweenness centrality asks how much traffic passes through a node. Picture everyone sending a message to everyone else along the shortest route. A node on many of those routes is a toll booth between parts of the network. Make a guess before anything is revealed.

Most people pick Hal or Rosa, the obvious hubs with six connections each. But Bea, with four, carries more than half of all the shortest paths between other pairs, because every journey from one side to the other goes through her. Close her and the network falls into two islands.

Formally, if $\sigma_{uv}$ is the number of shortest paths between $u$ and $v$, and $\sigma_{uv}(w)$ the number passing through $w$, then

\[C_B(w) = \sum_{u \neq v \neq w} \frac{\sigma_{uv}(w)}{\sigma_{uv}},\]

so each pair contributes the fraction of its shortest paths that $w$ lies on . This page uses Ulrik Brandes’s fast algorithm to compute it .A note for anyone comparing numbers. The betweenness values in my thesis and papers, and in Part 3, follow networkx: the sum runs over unordered pairs and is divided by $(n-1)(n-2)/2$, the number of pairs not involving $w$. A value of 1 means $w$ is on every shortest path between every other pair, as at the centre of a star. In this figure Bea’s 0.55 means that 55% of the pairs’ shortest-path traffic runs through her.

Milgram’s letters had a real toll booth: 16 of the 64 chains reached the stockbroker through the same clothing merchant . In a disease network, a high-betweenness condition sits between groups of conditions that otherwise rarely meet. The papers stressed this because betweenness did not simply track how common a condition was. Some rare conditions sat on many shortest paths, and Part 3 comes back to what that might mean.

Eigenvector centrality says you are important if your neighbours are important. That is circular, but the circle can be solved. Ask that each node’s score $x_v$ be proportional to the sum of its neighbours’ scores:

\[x_v = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{t \in M(v)} x_t = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{t \in V} a_{vt}\, x_t,\]

where $M(v)$ is the set of $v$’s neighbours. This is the eigenvector equation $A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x}$. Taking the largest eigenvalue guarantees, for a connected network, a solution with every score positive . To find it, give everyone a score of 1, let everyone pass their score to their neighbours, and repeat. I picture dye in water, pooling wherever the channels are densest until the pattern settles.

After one round the scores are just degree plus one, and Pat leads. By the fourth round Quinn has overtaken him. Quinn’s three friends are in the dense core and keep growing, while Pat’s six friends know no one else and have nothing to pass back. A modified version of this idea is at the heart of PageRank, the method Google was founded on . In my published work, degree and eigenvector centrality were highly correlated across conditions, while betweenness told a different story . That is part of why the papers leaned on betweenness.

Small worlds

Social networks are full of triangles, which should make them locally dense and slow to cross, like a world of tight villages. Yet the average distance between two people is tiny. How can a network be both cliquish and small?

In 1998 Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz answered with a simple model . Start with a ring of nodes, each joined to its nearest neighbours: the village, with lots of triangles and a long way round. Then, with probability $p$, cut one end of each edge loose and reattach it at random. At $p = 0$ you have the ring, and at $p = 1$ a random network.

The path length collapses long before the clustering does. A few rewired edges in a hundred act as shortcuts for everyone, but barely disturb the triangles. Watts and Strogatz called this window of high clustering and short paths a small world. Film actors, the western US power grid and the nervous system of the worm C. elegans all sat in it . So does the worldwide airline network, whose cities are on average 4.4 flights apart, with clustering of 0.62 against 0.049 when randomised .

The comparison against a random network of the same size is what matters, and my thesis did not make it. It described the TBI comorbidity network as “a relatively small-world structure” on the strength of its clustering and short paths. Rebuilding the analysis for this series, I compared it with 500 random networks with the same 25 nodes and 69 edges. Its average clustering is 0.38 (0.42 by the thesis’s convention), against 0.23 at random. Its average path length is 2.31, against 1.99. The clustering is well above chance, but the short paths say less, because a network this dense has short paths almost however it is wired. So the claim holds, modestly, and Part 3 tests the published network the same way.

Islands

Many networks are made of communities, groups of nodes more densely connected to each other than to the rest. Michelle Girvan and Mark Newman found them by using betweenness backwards . Edges between communities carry many shortest paths, so remove the busiest edge, recompute, and repeat. The network falls apart along its natural seams.

Part 3 uses a cousin of this method that removes the busiest nodes instead, then puts each back into every group it touched, so a condition can belong to more than one cluster.

One graph, many worlds

Once a problem is a graph, the same numbers can be computed for it, but what they mean depends on what the nodes and edges stand for. Choose what this small network represents.

Some of the most striking uses of graphs in medicine are recastings like this. In 2007 Goh and colleagues joined 1,284 disorders whenever one of 1,777 genes was implicated in both . That needed no new data, and it showed disorders clustering by shared genetic origin. Hidalgo and colleagues linked diseases that co-occurred in the histories of more than 30 million patients, and found that patients tended to develop diseases close in the network to those they already had . That is very nearly what my research built for mild TBI, on a much smaller scale, in what is now often called network medicine .

Hubs matter beyond medicine too. On networks where a few nodes have enormous numbers of contacts, an infection need not cross any threshold of infectiousness to persist , a formal version of why super-spreaders matter. Such networks are robust to random failures but fragile to the targeted loss of their hubs .

From people to diseases

So far the nodes have been obvious. Part 3 makes the least obvious recasting of all. The raw data is a table of people, each with conditions they do or do not have, and nobody hands you a network. You have to decide that conditions are the nodes, and that two are connected when they turn up in the same people.

Add everyone, and depression ends up connected to almost everything, partly because it is the most common condition here. A common condition co-occurs with many others by chance alone. What you want to know is whether two conditions occur together more than if they had nothing to do with each other. That depends on the people who have neither as well as those who have both, which is why Person 10, who adds nothing to the drawing, still matters. Part 3 answers it with a correlation coefficient for yes-or-no data and a significance test, and draws an edge only when the association is unlikely to be coincidence.

Once that network exists, every measure here becomes a question about brain injury. Would a hub be a condition so entangled that treating it might ease several others? Would a bridge sit between mental health and cardiovascular conditions, and between specialities that rarely talk? Would the network differ between younger and older people? And how much of it would reflect an injured brain, rather than who gets diagnosed, and who stays in a study long enough to be asked?

Some of those questions the study could answer and some it could not, and Part 3 tries to be clear about which are which.
