entry.content:
Five years after a mild brain injury, 225 people answered a set of questions about their health. This is what their answers look like when you stop reading them as lists and start reading them as a network.
Part 1The quiet injury Part 2Thinking in graphs Part 3A map of what comes after

Where we left off

Part 1 was about the injury. Most traumatic brain injuries are classed as mild, which describes how responsive someone was on arrival at hospital, not how the next ten years will go. For many people what follows is a long tail of other conditions, often several at once . Part 2 ended by turning a table of people and their conditions into a network, with conditions joined when they turn up together more often than chance would allow.

This part is about research that did that for mild traumatic brain injury (TBI from here on). It began as my undergraduate capstone at Krea University in 2023, supervised by Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar . It grew into three papers with him: on how common 26 conditions were five years after a mild TBI , on using comorbidity networks in TBI care , and on the networks themselves . The question running through them: after a mild TBI, which conditions keep company, and what does the web they form look like?

For this post I rebuilt the analysis from the public-use files and my original code; every number shown is from the papers or recomputed from the same data.

Where the numbers come from

A database of people who went to rehab

The data comes from the Traumatic Brain Injury Model Systems (TBIMS) National Database, set up in the United States in 1987. Its centres (currently 16) enrol people aged 16 or over who were admitted to hospital with a TBI and then had inpatient rehabilitation. They are interviewed one, two and five years after injury, and every five years after that . By March 2022 it held 19,045 people . Its public-use version is what an undergraduate without clinical access could work with.

Who is in it matters. Fewer than one in ten people hospitalised with a TBI need inpatient rehabilitation , so the “mild” injuries here are not the typical sports concussion. The Frontiers paper described them as typically involving intracranial pathology or post-traumatic amnesia (about ten days, on average, in the mild group) .

What makes an injury “mild”

They are mild by the Glasgow Coma Scale, described by Graham Teasdale and Bryan Jennett in 1974. It scores eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and movement (1 to 6), for a total from 3 to 15 . By convention 13 to 15 is mild, 9 to 12 moderate and 3 to 8 severe, as in the thesis and both papers . Its authors have since argued that the total suits groups better than individuals , which is how this study uses it.

From thousands to 225

The study used the five-year follow-up, chosen somewhat arbitrarily (as the thesis admitted) as far enough from the injury for the long tail to show . It needed people who answered the health questions at that interview.

The last step is the steep one. Of 1,915 people interviewed at five years, only 225 answered the health questions, because the questions were only asked in interviews between 2017 and 2019. The papers quote 223 to 228 depending on the question , but not why so few. I think it matters: the 225 are mostly people whose interview fell in a three-year window, not people especially keen to talk about their health.

The mild group as a whole is older than you might expect (median age 57 at injury) and mostly male, and falls are the commonest cause. That fits TBI in high-income countries . The 225 look much like the larger group, though they could differ in ways these few variables cannot show.

Numbers fall at every follow-up, and if the sickest drop out first, five-year figures understate what the injury does.

What was asked, and how it became data

The 26 conditions

The TBIMS interview includes questions modelled on the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), in the style of “Has a doctor or other health professional ever told you that you have…?”. Self-diagnosis was not accepted . My thesis used 25 conditions (all but “other heart conditions”); the BMC paper used all 26 .

From answers to ones and zeros

Anything other than a clear yes or no is set aside, so each condition rests on slightly fewer than 225 people. One wrinkle I cannot resolve: the Frontiers paper notes that a condition reported at an earlier follow-up was not asked about again . I would want to check how those answers carry forward before trusting any one person’s record.

So for each person and condition, the network gets a 1 (diagnosed), a 0 (never diagnosed) or a blank. Everything after this is arithmetic on those columns.

From people to pairs

Twenty-six conditions make $26 \times 25 / 2 = 325$ pairs. For each, we must decide whether the two are connected, and how strongly.

Four kinds of people

Take anxiety and depression. Everyone who answered both falls into one of four groups: both, anxiety only, depression only, or neither. Counting them gives a two-by-two contingency table.

Nineteen people have both. Is that a lot? If a third of people had each and the two were unrelated, a ninth would still have both by chance. So the real question is how the count compares with what independence predicts. Here chance predicts about six, so nineteen is about three times that.

Depression and hypertension are both common here (about a third and a half of people), and 34 people have both. That looks like a strong overlap, but chance also predicts about 34. Counting shared people, as the toy network in Part 2 did, would draw a thick edge; comparing with chance draws none.

The phi coefficient

The study used the phi coefficient, $\varphi$, the ordinary Pearson correlation between two columns of 1s and 0s. With $a$ people having both, $b$ only the first, $c$ only the second and $d$ neither,

\[\varphi = \frac{ad - bc}{\sqrt{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}}.\]

The product $ad$ grows when people have both or neither; $bc$ grows when they have one without the other. If the conditions are independent, these balance and $\varphi$ is zero. The denominator scales $\varphi$ to run from $-1$ (one present exactly when the other is absent) to $+1$ (always together).

For anxiety and depression, $\varphi = 0.48$, one of the strongest in the network and the value in the BMC paper . For depression and hypertension it is 0.005. For cataracts and depression it is $-0.08$, plausibly because cataracts come with age and depression was reported more by younger people here.

Why not just compare with chance directly?

The obvious alternative, which my thesis discussed, is the relative risk: the observed number with both divided by the number chance predicts. In 2009 César Hidalgo and colleagues compared the two measures on the hospital records of more than 30 million elderly Americans. Relative risk, they found, “overestimates relationships involving rare diseases”, while φ “underestimates the comorbidity between rare and common diseases” .

With two rare conditions, a handful of shared cases pushes the relative risk to 6 or more while $\varphi$ stays modest. With two common ones the relative risk has a ceiling: if half of everyone has each, they cannot co-occur more than twice as often as chance. The thesis chose $\varphi$ because, in a small sample, it does not make dramatic associations out of three or four people. The cost is that a rare condition can look weakly linked to a common one even when the link is real.

Where to draw the line

A correlation from a couple of hundred people will rarely be exactly zero, even for unrelated conditions. The standard test converts $\varphi$ into a $t$ statistic,

\[t = \frac{|\varphi|\sqrt{N-2}}{\sqrt{1-\varphi^2}},\]

where $N$ is the number of people behind the pair, compared with Student’s $t$ distribution with $N-2$ degrees of freedom. The BMC paper drew an edge when the one-sided p-value was below 0.01 , a $t$ above about 2.35. For around 200 people, that is a $\varphi$ of roughly 0.16 or more. The edge’s weight is $\varphi$ itself.

So the network depends on a choice as well as on the data: at 0.05 there are many more edges, at 0.001 only the strongest. Then there is the problem of many tests. Even if no pair were truly related, a 0.01 threshold across 325 pairs would let through about three edges by chance, and we cannot know which. A Bonferroni correction (dividing the threshold by 325) removes a good part of the edges but keeps the psychiatric core and the strongest links. So I think the strong edges are very unlikely to be flukes, while any single weak edge should be held lightly.

The thesis network was an earlier version of this analysis, with a different threshold: 25 conditions, 69 edges, diameter 5 . The paper’s has 26 conditions, 25 with at least one edge, and 65 edges . From here on I use the paper’s, which went through peer review.

The map

Here is the network for everyone. Stroke sits alone because none of its associations passed the threshold.

What I notice first is the dense knot of psychiatric and substance-use conditions, which holds the strongest associations: anxiety with panic attacks ($\varphi = 0.56$), attention deficit disorders with alcoholism (0.53), depression with panic attacks (0.49), anxiety with depression (0.48). Next is dementia with movement disorders (0.42), off on their own. Heart, lung and metabolic conditions form a looser web.

The matrix shows that most pairs are close to independent: only 65 of 325 are edges, and no negative association is strong enough to become one.

Reading the map

The whole network

The BMC paper did not report whole-network measures, so these are computed here.

A density of 0.22 means about one in five possible links is present. The average path is 2.31 steps (no two conditions are more than 4 apart), but random networks of this size have short paths too (2.05). Clustering is more telling: 0.36 here against 0.21 at random, so a condition’s neighbours are much more often linked to each other. High clustering with short paths is a small world , and this network is mildly one, as was the thesis network.

The assortativity is $+0.41$: well-connected conditions tend to link to each other. That is the psychiatric core again. With 25 nodes I would not lean on the exact value, but its sign matches what you can see.

The core

By degree or triangles, the psychiatric knot dominates. Panic attacks has the most links (10), then anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with 9 each. The same four sit in the most triangles (panic attacks in 25; depression and PTSD in 23 each). My thesis’s main conclusion was about exactly this: “the critical hub formed by the triangular relationship between mental disorders such as depression, anxiety, and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)” .

That is not surprising. Psychiatric conditions co-occur heavily in general, through shared risk factors and overlapping categories. It also fits the Frontiers finding that anxiety, depression and PTSD were among the commonest conditions after a mild TBI . What the network adds is that someone with one of them is quite likely to have several. Eigenvector centrality agrees, ranking the same four highest, and across conditions it tracks degree closely (a correlation of 0.93 ).

The bridges

Betweenness tells a different story, the one the paper followed. Make a guess first.

It is bipolar disorder. About 7% of people reported it, yet it has the second-highest betweenness (0.157), behind high cholesterol (0.186) and ahead of emphysema (0.133). Across conditions, betweenness was almost uncorrelated with prevalence ($r = 0.028$). As the paper put it, “despite exhibiting a low prevalence rate, a specific comorbidity could play a vital role in controlling disease transitions” .

Roger Guimerà and colleagues found that in the world’s airline network, “the most connected cities are not necessarily the most central” . Anchorage has few routes, but it is a gateway between an isolated region and the world. Bipolar disorder is linked into the psychiatric core and out to the heart (congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction, high cholesterol), so many shortest paths between the two pass through it.

A shortest path here is a chain of statistical associations, not a route a disease travels. It does not say that bipolar disorder leads to heart disease, or the reverse. Then again, it flags a place where psychiatry and cardiology, which rarely talk to each other, share patients.

Finding the neighbourhoods

To find groups in a principled way, the study borrowed a method from Camarillo-Ramirez and colleagues’ 2020 study of COVID-19 comorbidities in Mexico . It is a cousin of Girvan–Newman from Part 2 , but removes nodes instead of edges. Take out the node with the highest betweenness, recompute, and repeat until no node is above a threshold. The pieces left are the cluster cores. Each removed node then goes back into every cluster it had an edge to, so clusters can overlap, which for diseases seems right to me. The paper’s supplement shows it on seven nodes.

The BMC paper’s threshold was the median betweenness of the starting network . On the real network seven conditions are removed in turn: high cholesterol, emphysema, liver disease, bipolar disorder, rheumatoid arthritis, other heart conditions and attention deficit disorders. Rheumatoid arthritis starts modest, but once the conditions around it are gone it becomes the only link between its neighbours, and its score jumps to 0.48.

For everyone, the method finds the paper’s six clusters . The first is the psychiatric core with chronic pain and sleep disorder, plus five bridges: attention deficit disorders, bipolar disorder, emphysema, liver disease and rheumatoid arthritis. The second pairs diabetes and cataracts. The third is obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) with attention deficit disorders and rheumatoid arthritis; OCD is otherwise cut off from the core. The fourth is heart and lungs, around congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction and pneumonia. The fifth joins dementia, hypertension and movement disorders, and the sixth is osteoarthritis with high cholesterol.

Younger and older

The BMC paper then asked whether the network changes with age, since a fall at 75 and a road accident at 25 happen to different bodies. The Frontiers paper had found that, at five years, younger people reported depression more often, and older people hypertension, high cholesterol, cataracts and osteoarthritis . An earlier TBIMS study found much the same after moderate and severe injuries . So the paper split the 225 at age 50.

The younger network (91 people, 48 edges among 21 conditions) is held together by panic attacks, with 12 links, more than any condition elsewhere in the study. Its assortativity is negative ($-0.20$), like a hub with spokes. The older network (134 people, 37 edges among 22 conditions) is sparser, with assortativity $+0.44$, and dementia and movement disorders split off on their own.

The paper’s abstract leads with one difference: “bipolar disorder was seen as related to cardiovascular comorbidities, a pattern that was observed only in the young subjects” . This has precedent. The paper cites an American Heart Association statement that bipolar disorder predisposes young people to early cardiovascular disease, and a Korean cohort finding a raised risk of heart attack in young adults with it . OCD is linked with rheumatoid arthritis only in the younger group, which the paper connects to evidence that OCD may involve inflammation. And psychiatric links reach different places with age. Liver disease is linked to anxiety and PTSD only in the young; chronic pain to drug addiction, panic attacks and PTSD only in the old.

How much weight can these bear? The younger network rests on 91 people, and some of its conditions were reported by fewer than 11 of them. Stroke has seven links and the second-highest betweenness there, yet fewer than 11 younger people reported it, so a few people with several conditions could produce all of those edges. The bipolar–cardiovascular links fit the literature, but I would treat them as a hypothesis for a larger cohort, not a finding to act on. The paper itself warns that subgroup samples are smaller still .

What it means, and what it does not

The argument for using networks

No medicine prevents the secondary injuries after TBI, so much of care is managing what comes after. The perspective paper proposes “applying graph theory via the construction of disease comorbidity networks to identify high-risk patient groups, offer preventive care to affected populations, and reduce the disease burden” . The BMC paper adds that surveillance “for all possible sets of comorbidities is impractical” .

A network suggests where to look, and the paper’s main suggestion for practice is that a young patient with bipolar disorder after a mild TBI might have their heart checked earlier than usual. A larger study of mild TBI over up to ten years found raised risks of hypertension, diabetes and stroke, and called for screening . In Hidalgo’s study, patients tended to develop diseases close in the network to those they already had . If that holds after TBI, a comorbidity network is a rough map of where a patient might be heading. That is what I hope these networks could become; what they show now is much narrower.

What the study cannot tell us

It cannot say which came first. An edge says nothing about direction: “one won’t be able to establish if A preceded B or B preceded A” . Hidalgo’s study could infer direction from successive hospital visits ; one set of answers at five years cannot.

It cannot say the injury caused any of this. With no comparison group without a brain injury, we cannot tell which associations are specific to TBI; anxiety and depression go together almost everywhere. The paper replies that the patterns matter for people with mild TBI either way, and that brains may age faster after TBI, which complicates choosing controls . Both points are fair, but a control group is what would most change what this network can claim.

The conditions are self-reported, as diagnoses people recall being given. People who see doctors more get diagnosed with more, and memory is imperfect.

The people are a particular slice of TBI: hospitalised, then in inpatient rehabilitation in the United States, alive at five years and interviewed in 2017–2019. The Frontiers paper urged “sufficient caution” in generalising . If the sickest died or dropped out, the network looks healthier than reality.

The network depends on choices: the 1% threshold, $\varphi$ over relative risk, the median in the clustering. With 325 pairs tested, some edges are likely to be chance.

The numbers are small, especially by age. A condition reported by fewer than 11 people can gain or lose edges through one or two individuals.

Beyond the paper, and open questions

The thesis ended with a line I still stand by: “future research will focus on integrating data across TBI severities and longitudinal scales” . My original code had computed networks for other severities and years that were never analysed; here they are, outside anything the papers claim.

Each cell is a different set of people (53 to 384), so a row is not a fifteen-year story. What the grid does show is something like the psychiatric core in most cells, which makes me more inclined to think it is a stable feature of life after TBI.

Given the time and data, I would first follow the same people across years, so that edges could carry a direction. Depression at two years and heart problems at ten says far more than both at five. Second, I would build the same networks for matched people without a brain injury, where anything specific to TBI would have to show. Third, I would compare severities with enough people in each. The BMC paper’s stated aim, a large database of TBI patients followed across trauma centres in India , is the version I would most like to see.

Some questions I cannot answer. Is the psychiatric core a feature of brain injury, or of people in general? Is bipolar disorder a bridge to the heart in young people because of shared biology (inflammation, metabolism, the medicines used to treat it), or because of how they see doctors? Could betweenness help decide which specialists a patient sees, and would that help anyone? How much would the map change if everyone had been asked every year? I hope someone finds them curious enough to take up.

I am properly thankful to Dr Shyam Kumar Sudhakar, who supervised this work, conceived the papers that grew from it and did much of the writing. Thanks also to Shreya Sridhar, Satvika Char and Kathan Pandya, co-authors of the prevalence paper. The data come from the TBIMS National Database, funded by the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research, and from the people who answered its questions for years. The papers are open access: the networks in BMC Neurology , the prevalences in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience , and the perspective in the Brain Organoid and Systems Neuroscience Journal . The aggregated data behind every figure are in the site’s repository.

entry.content:
“Of course, we cannot give bread and butter for all 6000 patients. But we gave provisions for about 300 of them through various sources.” A manager heading outreach at the Schizophrenia Research Foundation, Chennai, on the months after India’s 2020 lockdown

That sentence is from an interview with a service provider at the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF), a non-government organisation in Chennai that provides care for a range of mental disorders and runs outreach services for rural communities. It is an odd thing to hear from a mental health organisation, because food is not usually counted as part of mental health care. The paper places it in a section on the burden of care at home, where the closure of the vocational centre and day-care came on top of job loss, pay cuts and rising debt for caregivers, and read in that context I find it hard to see where mental health care was supposed to stop and the rest of a family’s troubles begin.

This post is about my first research paper, The COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on mental health services: the provider perspective, published in the Journal of Public Health in October 2021 . It came out of a partnership between LEAD at Krea University and the University of Oxford, funded through the Global Challenges Research Fund’s India–Oxford Initiative, and it asked a fairly simple question: when the country shut down, what happened to community mental health services, and how did the people providing them keep them running?

I should say up front what my part in it was. The interviews, the focus group and the thematic analysis were done by my co-authors. My part was the literature review, which meant reading what had been reported from a geographically and socio-economically spread set of countries and using it to place the Chennai data in a wider context. The journal format is tight, about six pages, and most of the participants’ words had to be cut down to fragments. So, five years on, I wanted to write about it in a form where the quotes get more room and some of the numbers can be drawn out. How the study was done, and what was happening elsewhere at the time, come later in the post; Chennai comes first.

What broke

The first thing to go was access. In the two weeks of complete lockdown, in the paper’s words, “all services were affected”, and even once essential services resumed, patients could not easily reach the centre. Not every neighbourhood pharmacy stocked psychiatric medication, and some pharmacists that did were reluctant to dispense it. In smaller towns, psychiatric care was taken over for COVID-19 treatment. Rural patients were stopped by the police and fined on their way to refill prescriptions at SCARF, even when they showed the prescription.

“These are people who can’t even afford medicines… it felt painful that we were helpless.” A manager heading outreach efforts (P6)

Missed medication meant relapses of conditions like schizophrenia and mood disorders, often needing in-patient care, at exactly the time the centre had stopped admissions for fear of spreading COVID-19 inside the facility. One of the psychiatrists recalled handling “at least ten DESPERATE requests for admissions” (the capitals are in the paper). For patients who had been discharged and rehabilitated, the closure of the vocational centre took away a daily routine as well. The same psychiatrist described the “11 o clock tea” and the people they talked to, and added that most of them keep in touch with the staff regularly: “It was sad for them because this was their social life…” For people living with a chronic mental illness, I suspect that routine and that company were doing some of the work of treatment, even if nobody would have written them into a care plan.

What they built instead

What I find most interesting, reading the paper again, is how ordinary the adaptations were. Prescriptions were written on the official pad, signed, photographed and sent over WhatsApp, in line with the teleconsultation guidelines, and the consultants then spent time on the phone with pharmacists sorting out legibility, brand names, durations and substitutes. A health worker contacted the doctors of clients who were stuck in other districts and passed their prescriptions on. One psychiatrist described calling a pharmacist herself to get an overdue prescription honoured, asking them to dispense “for 1 week or 10 days” until she could see the patient.

That last detail is where my part of the paper meets the data. In the literature I was reviewing, one of the adaptations other health systems had made was to let patients keep using expired prescriptions . The same idea turns up in Chennai, except that here it was not a policy. It was one psychiatrist’s phone call, and it worked as long as she had the time and the pharmacist was willing.

The centre also ran a 24-hour helpline that linked new and existing patients to consultants and therapists. It was open to the public for distress calls, and the government displayed it in its media advertisements, so an NGO’s line became, in effect, part of the public response. The paper notes the cost plainly: existing staff and doctors had their working hours extended to handle the calls. It does not say whether that work was funded, so I will not guess, but it does make me wonder who carries the cost when a public service runs on an organisation’s goodwill.

Some of the infrastructure was even more personal. In the in-patient centres, staff used their own phones to set up video calls with families, partly to settle patients made anxious by the news coverage of COVID-19, and because many patients did not have smartphones. When staff or patients with cards and e-passes were stopped by the police, an administrator would be handed the phone to vouch for them. Decisions, emotional support and the sharing of load all happened in WhatsApp groups. Putting these together (and this is my synthesis, not the paper’s), a good part of the organisation’s continuity ran through its employees’ personal phones.

One of the most concrete changes in clinical practice was time. One psychiatrist described how a first consultation for a new patient, which used to take an hour, was now done in fifteen to twenty minutes.

A natural reading of that number is that care got worse, and I do not think the paper lets us say that. The time with the psychiatrist shrank, but the work was redistributed. A case manager took basic case details on a first phone call, and after the shorter consultation a case worker called the patient back to take the detailed history, which the psychiatrist then read at the next visit. The patient’s story was now held together by a case manager, a psychiatrist, a case worker and the electronic record, rather than by one person in one room. Whether that amounted to a loss, a different kind of care, or in some cases a better use of a psychiatrist’s hour is something interviews with providers alone cannot settle.

What it cost the people carrying it

The paper has a section on the providers’ personal costs, which I think is easy to skim past and should not be, partly because most of those costs follow directly from the adaptations above. The helpline extended working hours. The personal phones never went quiet. An administrative co-ordinator said that the hours after half past four used to be her own, and that she now checked her phone every three to five minutes “because I don’t want to miss anything”. Providers described feeling torn between giving good care and carrying out the new procedures, worried about bringing the virus home to their families, and saw less of their colleagues.

Some of it also cut across the usual hierarchy. The paper notes that responding meant “working across hierarchies”, and that two or three of the respondents held senior management positions on top of their other roles, which goes some way to explaining why a psychiatrist was negotiating with a pharmacist and an administrator was talking to the police.

The paper is also clear about why they kept going: commitment to care “was based on their personal motivation, a perceived sense of fulfilment”, despite the long hours and what it did to their work-life balance. I find that reassuring and a little worrying at once. If an organisation’s resilience rests on the motivation and overtime of its staff, how long can it last when the crisis does not end after two weeks? The study did not measure burnout, so I can only leave that as a question.

Telemedicine, and the room it took away

Telemedicine was the largest single change. The paper’s abstract says it enabled an expansion of both the service and its clientele, as well as efficiency, and the gains were real. It also changed what a therapy session was like, for both sides.

The phrase “casualization” is the one I keep coming back to.The abstract uses “casualization of therapy”; the discussion uses “casualization of the exchange between service provider and patient”. Some clients, as the paper puts it, took phone sessions as “a friendly catch-up call rather than a teletherapy session”. A case worker said that when she asked clients why they had not called, they told her they thought the centre had called “just to ask ‘How are you doing? Are you taking medicine’”. I wonder whether that is partly a side effect of the relationship itself. Years of check-in calls teach people that a call from SCARF is a kind voice asking how they are, and when therapy arrived through the same phone, it is not surprising that some heard it the same way. The work of keeping to a schedule also moved from the client to the counsellor, which the paper counts as an additional burden.

The cost I did not appreciate until I sat with these quotes is privacy. A consulting room is, among other things, a private space, and it is easy not to notice that until it is gone. One outreach manager described families where “women and children have faced a lot of issues”, and asked how a woman could talk about her husband to someone over the phone when the husband was in the room. Moving care into the home moved it, for some women, into the very place where the problem was. The paper makes the general point in its discussion, that privacy issues may matter most “in planning for communities with space constraints”, and I think that one line deserves more weight than its place in the discussion suggests. I should be careful about how far it goes, though: this is one provider’s account of what women could not say, not the women’s own words, and the study cannot tell us how common it was.

Privacy failed at the other end of the line too. The counsellor whose children “would wonder why the person on the other end was crying so much” was describing a cost to herself, and the paper files it that way, under her loss of privacy and family time. I think it was also a cost to the person crying, whose distress was audible to a stranger’s parents and children without anyone having chosen that. The same outreach manager noticed his own position: “I am sitting and talking to you in a sound proof room, but that is not possible for everyone.”In the paper, that remark sits in a passage about public outreach and training moving online, where it was harder to keep up two-way communication with community health workers in rural districts. He goes on: “Women in rural areas were not comfortable with gadgets.” I have used only the first sentence here, as an observation about privacy.

The crowded home that took privacy away also turned family into a resource. Compliance was better where family members became co-therapists, and one patient was rehabilitated with the help of her 10-year-old child. The paper presents that as a success, and it may well have been one. I would only ask, as a question rather than a criticism, what we are asking of a ten-year-old when we make them part of their parent’s treatment.

Relationships, responsiveness, resilience

When the paper pulls these threads together, it names “three crucial elements in continuity and quality service delivery: relationships, responsiveness and resilience” .

Two of the three were in place before the pandemic. The relationships had been built over many years, partly through educating patients and families, and the providers felt that this psycho-education showed its value in how well patients kept to treatment. The resilience drew on lessons from earlier floods, the tsunami and cyclones, and on prior experience with tele-psychiatry, which the paper says made the move online easier. Responsiveness is the one that happened during the crisis, in the continual adaptations described above. I suspect the first two are what made the third possible: provisions can only reach 300 patients if someone already knows who those patients are. The paper does not say which lessons from the earlier disasters carried over, and I would genuinely like to know, because a pandemic is a different kind of disaster, long and everywhere at once, with no unaffected place from which help can arrive.

The view from outside

None of this was unique to Chennai in kind. In October 2020 the World Health Organization published a survey of 130 countries , and the headline figure was blunt.

The literature I was reading at the time was largely about hospitals and health systems. From China there were accounts of psychiatric hospitals reorganising around infection control , and elsewhere descriptions of how inpatient psychiatry and psychiatric care more broadly had been reshaped in the first months . A piece in The Lancet Psychiatry set out how mental health care should change as a consequence . Adaptation was not absent from this work: telecommunication platforms, electronic prescriptions, the continued use of expired prescriptions, isolation and liaison psychiatry were all being reported . What was missing was adaptation in community care run by NGOs, which matters in India because mental health outreach to communities and vulnerable groups here was pioneered by NGOs, and their lessons have proved useful to the public system .

Reading that literature against the Chennai interviews, a few comparisons stand out to me. The expired-prescription policy elsewhere and the psychiatrist’s phone call to a pharmacist are one. Another is the observation that services for rural and older populations, which were always harder to reach, got worse during the pandemic , set against rural patients being fined on their way to collect medicine. A third is the WHO’s split in telemedicine adoption between high- and low-income countries, set against the women in shared homes who could not speak freely on a call. In each case the broad pattern in the literature shows up in Chennai, but at the scale of a single person and a single phone call.

In India specifically, services were disrupted by the nationwide lockdown in March 2020, and the government released guidelines to move to telemedicine . Tele-psychiatry had raised concerns about patient dynamics, proper diagnosis and legal issues , though it had worked in some contexts .

How the study was done

SCARF is, in the paper’s words, a training centre for psychiatry, psychology and psychiatric social work, and a training partner for public mental health services, as well as a provider . That breadth meant one organisation’s staff could speak about many kinds of service, from inpatient wards to rural outreach. The paper also notes the organisation’s prior experience with tele-psychiatry, which probably left it better placed than many.

The people interviewed included managers of clinical services, administrative staff, psychiatrists, social workers, a psychologist and research staff, with between three and more than twenty years at the organisation. Their accounts covered February to December 2020, and the fieldwork itself ran over December 2020 and January 2021. One small thing I should flag: the paper says ten providers were selected and that one interview could not be scheduled, yet quotes are labelled up to P10, so the numbering may not map neatly onto the interviews that took place.

What this study cannot tell us

The paper is direct about its main limitation: “Though limited to a single NGO and to providers, insights from a variety of services within mental healthcare was gleaned” . Both halves of that sentence matter. One organisation based in one city, however broad its services and however far its outreach reaches, is not Indian community mental health care as a whole. And the people interviewed were the people delivering care, not receiving it. We do not know how the shortened consultation felt from the patient’s side, or whether the phone sessions that providers worried were too casual felt that way to the people on the other end.

It is also a retrospective account. The interviews were conducted at the end of 2020 about the months that came before, and what people remember of a crisis, and how they make sense of it afterwards, is not quite the same as what happened at the time. I would rather say that plainly than have the post read as a claim about more than the study can support.

Coming back to it

The paper ends by arguing that these insights are crucial for planning resilient community-based mental health care, and the wider literature at the time was saying something similar: that the pandemic was an opportunity to reform mental health care in India , and that health systems needed to be built with preparedness in mind . The paper is specific about what that would mean: bringing care for people with mental illness into government and city disaster planning, including housing, transport and medication; sensitising the police and other enforcing authorities to their needs, which I read as coming out of the patients fined at checkpoints; training health workers for isolation, infection and relocation; and preparing patients and caregivers for how to manage care during a disaster.

Reading it again now, the question I keep returning to is which of these adaptations outlasted the pandemic, and whether anyone asked patients what the phone intake, the shorter consultation and the WhatsApp prescription changed for them. I do not have an answer, and I suspect it needs the patient and family perspective this study did not have. That includes the families who were not among the 300, and I would like to know what they made of the year.

It was my first time seeing my name on a paper, and I am properly thankful to my co-authors, Sapna Nair, Preethi Kannan, Ananya Raju, John Mathew and Padmavati Ramachandran, for bringing me in, and to the providers at SCARF who gave their time to be interviewed at the end of a very hard year. The full paper is available from the Journal of Public Health.
